sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: A network team deploys a pair of third-party network virtual appliances (NVAs) in a hub virtual network. The team must use a single load-balancing rule to distribute all TCP and UDP flows arriving on every port to the NVAs. Which configuration meets the requirement?
opzione_a: An internal Standard Load Balancer with a load-balancing rule set to protocol All and port 0
opzione_b: A public Standard Load Balancer with a load-balancing rule set to protocol All and port 0
opzione_c: An internal Standard Load Balancer with a separate load-balancing rule for each port from 1 through 65535
opzione_d: An internal Basic Load Balancer with a load-balancing rule set to protocol All and port 0
spiegazione: Correct (a): A High Availability (HA) ports rule is created by setting the frontend and backend ports to 0 and the protocol to All. HA ports load-balancing rules are available only on an internal Standard Load Balancer, and they balance all TCP and UDP flows regardless of port number. This is the documented pattern for scaling and providing high availability to NVAs. Wrong (b): HA ports are not supported on a public load balancer; the feature is documented as available only for an internal Standard Load Balancer. Wrong (c): This does not use a single rule, and creating per-port rules is exactly the operational problem HA ports were designed to eliminate. Wrong (d): Basic Load Balancer does not support HA ports at all; the SKU comparison lists HA Ports as 'Not available' for Basic.
tags: load balancer,ha ports,internal load balancer,standard sku,nva

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: Contoso publishes a Remote Desktop Gateway (RD Gateway) farm behind a public Standard Load Balancer. Users cannot establish RD Gateway sessions reliably. You must configure the load-balancing rule to use the three-tuple distribution mode that Azure recommends to resolve the known incompatibility between Azure Load Balancer and RD Gateway. Which Session persistence value should you select in the Azure portal?
spiegazione: Correct (c): 'Client IP and protocol' is the three-tuple distribution mode (source IP, destination IP, and protocol type). Microsoft documents that source IP affinity with client IP and protocol solves an incompatibility between Azure Load Balancer and RD Gateway. Wrong (a): 'None' is the default hash-based mode and uses the five-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol), which provides no session persistence across new sessions because the source port changes. Wrong (b): 'Client IP' is the two-tuple mode (source IP and destination IP), not the three-tuple mode named in the requirement. Wrong (d): 'Client IP and port' is not a valid session persistence option in Azure Load Balancer; the only options are None, Client IP, and Client IP and protocol.
tags: load balancer,session persistence,distribution mode,source ip affinity,rd gateway

domanda: After a security team applies a custom network security group (NSG) to the subnet that hosts the backend virtual machines of a Standard Load Balancer, the backend pool health shows every instance as unhealthy and clients receive no response. The NSG contains a custom inbound rule at priority 4000 that denies all traffic. You must restore the health probes with the least administrative effort. What should you do?
opzione_a: Create an inbound allow rule for the probe port with the source service tag Internet at a priority lower than 4000.
opzione_b: Create an outbound allow rule to destination 168.63.129.16 on the probe port at a priority lower than 4000.
opzione_c: Create a route table with a route for 168.63.129.16/32 that has a next hop type of Internet and associate it with the subnet.
opzione_d: Create an inbound allow rule for the probe port with the source service tag AzureLoadBalancer at a priority lower than 4000.
spiegazione: Correct (d): All IPv4 Load Balancer health probes originate from source IP address 168.63.129.16. The AzureLoadBalancer service tag identifies this source address in an NSG. Because NSG rules are evaluated by priority and a lower number takes precedence, an inbound allow rule for the probe port sourced from the AzureLoadBalancer tag with a priority number lower than 4000 is evaluated before the custom deny-all rule, so probes reach the VMs. Wrong (a): The Internet service tag does not represent 168.63.129.16, which is a virtual public IP of the host node rather than an internet source; the rule would not permit the probe. Wrong (b): The probe is inbound traffic to the virtual machine, so an outbound NSG rule does not unblock it. Wrong (c): 168.63.129.16 is a virtual IP of the host node and is not subject to user-defined routes, so a UDR cannot fix this; the failure is caused by NSG filtering, not routing.

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: You enable Floating IP on a load-balancing rule of a Standard Load Balancer so that multiple application instances on a backend virtual machine can reuse the same backend port. Which additional configuration must you perform inside the guest operating system of each backend virtual machine?
opzione_a: Add a secondary IP configuration to the virtual machine network interface and assign the frontend IP address of the load balancer to it.
opzione_b: Add a loopback interface and configure it with the frontend IP address of the load balancer.
opzione_c: Assign an instance-level public IP address to each virtual machine network interface.
opzione_d: Change the default gateway of the virtual machine to the frontend IP address of the load balancer.
spiegazione: Correct (b): With Floating IP enabled, Azure preserves the load balancer frontend IP address as the destination in the packet instead of rewriting it to the VM IP address. For the VM to accept that traffic, the guest OS must add a loopback interface configured with the frontend IP address, and (on Windows) the interfaces must use the weak host model; the guest firewall must also allow the frontend port. Wrong (a): The frontend IP address is not added as a secondary IP configuration on the Azure NIC; Floating IP is configured in the load-balancing rule plus the guest OS loopback, and Floating IP is not supported on secondary IP configurations for load balancing scenarios. Wrong (c): An instance-level public IP provides outbound connectivity and direct inbound addressing; it has nothing to do with accepting frontend-addressed packets. Wrong (d): Changing the default gateway is not part of the Floating IP configuration and would break the VM's normal routing through the Azure fabric.
tags: load balancer,floating ip,direct server return,loopback,port reuse

domanda: An engineer creates a public IP address named pip1 by using the Basic SKU, then attempts to add pip1 as the frontend IP configuration of a newly created Standard Load Balancer named lb1. The operation fails. The application must remain reachable on the IP address that pip1 currently uses. What should you do?
opzione_a: Delete lb1 and recreate it by using the Basic SKU, then associate pip1 with its frontend IP configuration.
opzione_b: Associate pip1 with a NAT gateway and add the NAT gateway to the frontend IP configuration of lb1.
opzione_c: Add pip1 to a new public IP prefix and reference the public IP prefix from the frontend IP configuration of lb1.
opzione_d: Set the allocation method of pip1 to Static, upgrade pip1 to the Standard SKU, and then associate it with the frontend IP configuration of lb1.
spiegazione: Correct (d): The SKU of the public IP must match the SKU of the load balancer. When using a public Standard Load Balancer, the public IP must be Standard; Basic public IPs are not supported on a Standard Load Balancer, and Basic and Standard SKU IPs and load balancers cannot be mixed. Microsoft's upgrade guidance directs you to set the allocation method to Static (otherwise the address is lost when it is disassociated) and then upgrade the public IP to the Standard SKU, which preserves the address. Wrong (a): Basic Load Balancer was retired on September 30, 2025, is unsupported, and carries no SLA, so recreating lb1 as Basic is not an acceptable resolution. Wrong (b): A NAT gateway provides outbound-only connectivity for a subnet; it cannot be used as the frontend IP configuration of a load balancer. Wrong (c): A public IP prefix is a contiguous range of Standard SKU public IP addresses that Azure allocates; you cannot add an existing Basic public IP to a prefix, so this would not preserve the current address.
tags: load balancer,sku mismatch,public ip,standard sku,basic retirement,troubleshooting

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: A load-balancing rule on a Standard Load Balancer references a backend pool that contains three virtual machines. A configuration error causes the health probe to fail on all three virtual machines at the same time. What happens to the TCP connections that were already established through the load balancer?
opzione_a: The established TCP flows continue, but no new flows are sent to the backend pool.
opzione_b: All established TCP flows are immediately terminated with a TCP reset.
opzione_c: The established TCP flows continue only if TCP Reset on idle is disabled on the load-balancing rule.
opzione_d: The established TCP flows are redistributed to the next healthy backend pool referenced by the load balancer.
spiegazione: Correct (a): When all instances probe down, no new flows are sent to the backend pool, but Standard Load Balancer allows established TCP flows to continue, given that the backend pool has more than one backend instance. Wrong (b): Terminating all existing TCP flows when all probes are down is Basic Load Balancer behavior, and it is the classic misconception carried over to Standard. Wrong (c): TCP Reset on idle is a separate feature that controls whether a bidirectional TCP RST is sent when the idle timeout is reached; it does not govern probe-down behavior. Wrong (d): A load-balancing rule targets a single backend pool and there is no automatic failover to another pool; when all probes are down the load balancer simply stops sending new flows.
tags: load balancer,health probe,probe down behavior,standard sku,tcp flows

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: You are documenting the differences between the Azure Load Balancer SKUs for a migration plan. Which capabilities are available with a Standard Load Balancer but NOT with a Basic Load Balancer? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_b: Outbound rules that declaratively define SNAT
opzione_c: Zone-redundant and zonal frontend IP configurations
opzione_d: Inbound NAT rules for port forwarding to a specific virtual machine
spiegazione: Correct (a): The SKU comparison lists health probe protocols as TCP, HTTP, and HTTPS for Standard, but only TCP and HTTP for Basic. Correct (b): Outbound rules provide declarative outbound NAT configuration and are listed as 'Not available' for Basic. Correct (c): Availability zone support (zone-redundant or zonal frontend IP configurations for inbound and outbound traffic) is a Standard-only capability; Basic is documented as not compatible with availability zones. Wrong (d): Inbound NAT rules are a core load balancer component supported by both SKUs, so this is not a difference. Wrong (e): TCP health probes are supported by both SKUs; only HTTPS probes are exclusive to Standard.
tags: load balancer,sku comparison,standard sku,basic sku,availability zones,outbound rules

domanda: Backend virtual machines behind a public Standard Load Balancer begin failing new outbound connections to an external API during peak hours. Diagnostics indicate SNAT port exhaustion. The load balancer currently has a single frontend public IP address that is used for both inbound load-balancing rules and implicit outbound SNAT. Which actions can mitigate the SNAT port exhaustion? Select all that apply. Each correct answer presents part of the solution.
opzione_a: Add more public IP addresses, or a public IP prefix, to the frontend of an outbound rule.
opzione_b: Set disableOutboundSnat to true on the load-balancing rule and configure an outbound rule with a higher Ports per instance value.
opzione_c: Associate a NAT gateway with the subnet that contains the backend virtual machines.
opzione_d: Change the session persistence of the load-balancing rule to Client IP.
opzione_e: Enable Floating IP on the load-balancing rule.
spiegazione: Correct (a): Each public IP address added to the frontend of an outbound rule contributes up to 64,000 extra ephemeral ports for the load balancer to use as SNAT ports, and a public IP prefix contributes 64,000 ports per address it contains. Correct (b): To tune the SNAT port allocation of an address that is also used for inbound, the automatic outbound NAT programmed by the load-balancing rule must first be disabled by setting disableOutboundSnat to true so the outbound rule can take control; you can then raise the allocation above the default. Correct (c): Azure NAT Gateway is the recommended outbound method, takes precedence over load balancer outbound connectivity, and uses dynamic port allocation that does not have the same SNAT port exhaustion concerns. Wrong (d): Session persistence (Client IP, two-tuple) only changes how inbound flows are distributed across the backend pool; it has no effect on outbound SNAT port allocation. Wrong (e): Floating IP changes inbound destination IP mapping for port reuse scenarios; it allocates no SNAT ports, and with Floating IP enabled the application must still use the primary IP configuration of the NIC for outbound.

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: You are configuring a health probe for a public Standard Load Balancer that fronts a set of web servers in a subnet protected by a network security group. Select the correct value for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Health probe protocols supported by a Standard Load Balancer: [TCP only | TCP and HTTP | TCP, HTTP, and HTTPS]
opzione_b: Source IP address of an IPv4 health probe: [168.63.129.16 | 169.254.169.254 | The frontend IP address of the load balancer]
opzione_c: Network security group service tag that permits health probe traffic: [AzureLoadBalancer | VirtualNetwork | AzurePlatformDNS]
opzione_d: HTTP status code that marks an HTTP health probe as healthy: [200 | Any 2xx or 3xx code | 200 or 404]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - 'TCP, HTTP, and HTTPS': Standard Load Balancer supports TCP, HTTP, and HTTPS probe protocols; Basic supports only TCP and HTTP, which makes 'TCP and HTTP' the Basic-SKU distractor. 'TCP only' is incorrect for either SKU. Dropdown 2 - '168.63.129.16': All IPv4 Load Balancer health probes originate from 168.63.129.16, a Microsoft-owned virtual public IP used in all regions and national clouds. 169.254.169.254 is the Azure Instance Metadata Service endpoint, not the probe source. The frontend IP address is never the probe source. Dropdown 3 - 'AzureLoadBalancer': This service tag identifies 168.63.129.16 in network security groups and permits health probe traffic by default. VirtualNetwork covers virtual network address space and peered/on-premises ranges, not the probe source. AzurePlatformDNS is used to control Azure-provided DNS traffic. Dropdown 4 - '200': An HTTP/HTTPS probe is marked up only when the instance responds with HTTP status 200 within the timeout period; any other code (for example 403, 404, or 500) fails the probe, so the 2xx/3xx range and '200 or 404' are incorrect.

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: Fabrikam must load balance every TCP and UDP flow on all ports to a set of network virtual appliances by using one load-balancing rule, and must later add more load-balancing rules that target the same backend IP configurations on the same frontend IP configuration. Select the correct value for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Load balancer type required: [Public Standard | Internal Standard | Internal Basic]
opzione_b: Protocol setting in the load-balancing rule: [TCP | UDP | All]
opzione_d: Floating IP setting required on the rules: [Disabled | Enabled | Not applicable]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - 'Internal Standard': HA ports load-balancing rules are available only for an internal Standard Load Balancer. HA ports are not supported on public load balancers or on the Basic SKU. Dropdown 2 - 'All': An HA ports rule is configured with the protocol set to All so that the load balancer balances all TCP and UDP flows. Selecting TCP or UDP alone would restrict the rule to a single protocol. Dropdown 3 - '0': HA ports rules are configured by setting the frontend and backend ports to 0, which represents all ports. Port 80 would balance a single port, and 65535 is only the highest individual port number, not a wildcard. Dropdown 4 - 'Enabled': Combining an HA ports load-balancing rule with a non-HA ports load-balancing rule that points to the same backend IP configurations is not supported on a single frontend IP configuration unless both rules have Floating IP enabled. A non-floating HA ports configuration allows no other load-balancing rule on the load balancer resource, so 'Disabled' would block the additional rules.
tags: load balancer,ha ports,floating ip,internal load balancer,load balancing rule,hotspot

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda: A public Standard Load Balancer has a NIC-based backend pool that contains 60 virtual machines. The load-balancing rule has default port allocation enabled (disableOutboundSnat is set to false) and no outbound rules are configured. Select the correct value for each dropdown.
opzione_a: Default SNAT ports allocated per virtual machine with one frontend public IP address: [1024 | 512 | 256]
opzione_b: Default SNAT ports allocated per virtual machine after a second frontend public IP address is added: [512 | 1024 | 2048]
opzione_c: Default SNAT ports allocated per virtual machine after a third frontend public IP address is added: [1024 | 1536 | 2048]
opzione_d: Ephemeral ports contributed by each frontend public IP address: [64000 | 65535 | 1024]
spiegazione: Dropdown 1 - '512': The default SNAT port preallocation table assigns ports based on backend pool size for a single frontend IP. A pool of 60 instances falls in the 51-100 range, which receives 512 ports. 1024 applies to pools of 1-50 instances and 256 applies to pools of 101-200 instances. Dropdown 2 - '1024': Each backend receives the number of ports defined by the table per frontend IP, so a second frontend IP adds another 512 ports for a total of 1024. Dropdown 3 - '1024': Default port allocation is capped at a maximum of 1024 ports per backend instance, computed as MIN(default ports based on pool size * number of frontend IPs, 1024). Adding a third frontend IP therefore does not increase the allocation beyond 1024. Dropdown 4 - '64000': When a public IP address is added as a frontend IP to a load balancer, 64,000 ports are eligible for SNAT. Although every IP address has 65,535 ports by definition, only 64,000 are usable ephemeral SNAT ports, and 1024 is the default per-instance allocation cap rather than a per-IP total.

domanda:
Litware runs a public Standard Load Balancer named lb1 in front of three web servers. The load-balancing rule forwards TCP port 80 on the frontend to port 80 on the backend, and it references an HTTP health probe that uses port 8080 with a request path of /health. Backend health currently shows all three instances as unhealthy, and you are reviewing the configuration. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true.
1. An HTTP health probe is marked healthy only when the backend instance responds with HTTP status 200 within the timeout period.
2. The configuration is invalid because a health probe must use the same port as the backend port of the load-balancing rule.
3. If you reconfigure the probe to use the HTTPS protocol on port 8080, the certificate chain presented by the backend must use a minimum signature hash of SHA256.
opzione_a: An HTTP health probe is marked healthy only when the backend instance responds with HTTP status 200 within the timeout period.
opzione_b: The configuration is invalid because a health probe must use the same port as the backend port of the load-balancing rule.
opzione_c: If you reconfigure the probe to use the HTTPS protocol on port 8080, the certificate chain presented by the backend must use a minimum signature hash of SHA256.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes: An HTTP/HTTPS probe is marked up when the instance responds with HTTP status 200 within the timeout period. Any other response code (such as 403, 404, or 500), no response within the timeout, or a TCP reset causes the probe to fail. Statement 2 - No: The application port and the probe port are not required to be the same. Microsoft's design guidance states that in some scenarios it can be desirable for the probe port to differ from the application port, although using the same port is generally recommended. The probe port must simply be a port the VM is actually listening on, which is the more likely root cause here. Statement 3 - Yes: The HTTPS probe requires the use of certificates that have a minimum signature hash of SHA256 in the entire chain.
tags: load balancer,health probe,http probe,https probe,probe port,troubleshooting

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda:
An internal Standard Load Balancer named ilb1 has a frontend private IP address in subnet1 of a virtual network named vnet1. The backend pool of ilb1 is NIC-based and contains virtual machines in subnet2 of vnet1. No NAT gateway is deployed, and the backend virtual machines have no instance-level public IP addresses. Evaluate whether each of the following statements is true.
1. A virtual machine in the backend pool of ilb1 can successfully initiate an outbound flow to the frontend IP address of ilb1.
2. An on-premises client connected through a site-to-site VPN can reach the frontend IP address of ilb1.
3. Adding a virtual machine to the backend pool of ilb1 gives that virtual machine outbound internet connectivity.
opzione_a: A virtual machine in the backend pool of ilb1 can successfully initiate an outbound flow to the frontend IP address of ilb1.
opzione_b: An on-premises client connected through a site-to-site VPN can reach the frontend IP address of ilb1.
opzione_c: Adding a virtual machine to the backend pool of ilb1 gives that virtual machine outbound internet connectivity.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No: An outbound flow from a backend virtual machine to the frontend of an internal load balancer is a documented limitation and fails. This is the classic 'VM cannot reach its own load balancer frontend' behavior. Statement 2 - Yes: An internal load balancer distributes traffic to resources inside a virtual network and is explicitly documented for private network connectivity scenarios, such as accessing a load balancer frontend from an on-premises network in a hybrid deployment. The frontend is never exposed to an internet endpoint, but it is reachable over VPN or ExpressRoute. Statement 3 - No: Outbound connectivity is not available for an internal Standard Load Balancer until it is explicitly declared through instance-level public IP addresses, a NAT gateway on the backend subnet, or by associating the backend pool members with an outbound-only public load balancer configuration. Membership in an internal load balancer backend pool provides no outbound internet access.
tags: load balancer,internal load balancer,outbound connectivity,hybrid,backend pool

sotto_argomento: Configure an internal or public load balancer
domanda:
Case study: Fabrikam operates a hub-and-spoke topology in the East US region. The hub virtual network contains three third-party firewall network virtual appliances (NVAs), each with a single network interface that has one IP configuration. Spoke virtual networks force-tunnel all traffic to the hub by using user-defined routes. Fabrikam must ensure that all TCP and UDP traffic on every port is distributed across the three NVAs, that an NVA that stops responding is automatically removed from rotation, and that ingress and egress traffic for a given flow traverses the same NVA instance.

Which configuration should Fabrikam deploy in the hub virtual network?
opzione_a: An internal Standard Load Balancer with an HA ports load-balancing rule and a health probe, referenced as the next hop of the spoke user-defined routes.
opzione_b: A public Standard Load Balancer with an HA ports load-balancing rule and a health probe, referenced as the next hop of the spoke user-defined routes.
opzione_c: An internal Standard Load Balancer with individual load-balancing rules for TCP ports 80 and 443 and Floating IP enabled, referenced as the next hop of the spoke user-defined routes.
opzione_d: The NVAs placed in the backend pools of both a public Standard Load Balancer and an internal Standard Load Balancer, with the internal load balancer referenced as the next hop of the spoke user-defined routes.
spiegazione: Correct (a): This is the documented NVA high availability pattern. An HA ports rule on an internal Standard Load Balancer balances all TCP and UDP flows on all ports, per-instance health probes provide fast failover by removing an unhealthy NVA from rotation, and in exactly this hub-and-spoke force-tunnel design an HA ports rule provides flow symmetry for ingress and egress traffic. Flow symmetry is supported here because each backend instance has one NIC with one IP configuration. Wrong (b): HA ports load-balancing rules are available only for an internal Standard Load Balancer and are not supported on a public load balancer, so this configuration cannot be created. Wrong (c): Rules for TCP 80 and 443 balance only those two ports and no UDP traffic, which fails the requirement to distribute all TCP and UDP traffic on every port. Wrong (d): Flow symmetry is not supported when NVAs are placed between a public and an internal load balancer, because two independent load balancer components make uncoordinated distribution decisions. Gateway Load Balancer would be the alternative for that topology.
tags: load balancer,ha ports,nva,flow symmetry,hub and spoke,internal load balancer,case study
